newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil equities analysts now in demand.
newsitem.headline: Brazil equities analysts now in demand.

text.p: Once relegated to dusty back offices, Brazil's equity analysts are now the target of corporate headhunters and hotly sought after by rival banks anxious to build up their own research departments.
Huge demand for solid insight on listed Brazilian companies has catapulted analysts to an enviable position within Brazil's competitive financial industry.

"In the past analysts were forced to move to another area of the bank if they planned on moving up," said Paulo Vasconcellos, ING Barings' research department chief in Brazil. "Being an analyst was seen as a stepping-stone in one's career," he said.

Vasconcellos belongs to a select group of analysts who have helped turn around the industry's attitude towards research departments. After working for Merrill Lynch for over four years, he was hired in August to rebuild the ING Barings research team after it lost 14 analysts and salesmen to Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.

The growing demand for corporate information and the improved status of analysts followed the success of Brazil's two-year-old anti-inflation plan and the favorable prospects it has created for local companies.

"Before, any information we sent to clients was welcome, because knowlege of the country was scarce," said Vasconcellos. "Today, an analyst must add value, his recommendations must be solid and very well argued."
Vasconcellos said an analyst must not only advise clients about opportunities in the stock market but must also function as a "business generator."
"As we have greater knowledge of Brazilian firms, we are able to help in the case of an IPO or a block trade, or even advise the company in its investor relations," he said.

New responsibilities have helped boost salaries. Headhunter Alfredo Assuncao said a senior analyst will earn on average between $100,000 and $120,000 a year and some will make up to $300,000, including an annual bonus.
Assuncao, who works for Financial Executive Search Association (FESA), is currently looking for candidates to fill eight new research and sales positions.
Even banks focusing on portfolio management are seeking to build up their research teams.
"We have more analysts on the buy side all the time," said Saulo Holzman, who left Alliance Capital four months ago to set up the research department at BBA Capital.
Analysts' luck began to change in 1991, when the so-called Annex Four code regulating foreign investment in local stocks, debentures and privatization bonds was introduced.
Since then $14.5 billion in net foreign investment has flowed to local stock markets under the Annex Four regime.
With foreign interest on the rise, local banks were forced to offer special services and help clients make their choices among Brazil's 500 listed companies.

"The equity market became extremely attractive with the economic stabilization. And to invest in equities, you need a good research department," said FESA's Assuncao. He noted foreign investment banks also have been opening offices in Brazil, which has increased demand for local analysts.
While Assuncao expects the hunt for analysts to slow after the present shortage has been filled, Vasconcellos predicts demand will remain firm as the Brazilian economy continues to grow.
